title: Roy Acuff, Ernest Tubb and the Nashville sound; the Doughboys' unique pride
summary: Parker liked Acuff and Tubb personally but saw Nashville as a different, vaudeville-like music. The Doughboys saw themselves as a unique group and were concerned when he left.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well, how did you regard yourself via people like Roy Acuff and the Grand Ole Opry crew?

Oh, we liked them personally. Roy Acuff for a while was there in Fort Worth when he wrote Walking the Floor. Is that the Walking the Floor over you guys? Or Ernst Tubb. Ernst Tubb. I remember Ernst Tubb. We liked very much personally, the Walking the Floor over you. We kind of looked over there. We smiled. We thought that was kind of vaudeville or something really, you know, and we liked him okay, but he's kind of just a personality singer. The same way now, I'd be tolerant. Elvis Presley, you know, he's alright. Knock the pool guy, but he's something, another genre.
And you regarded the Nashville group of people as another kind of music?
Probably so, probably so. We, I don't know. We were, we had by.

now kind of we developed ourselves into a little unique category. We were very proud of our group. We were very very proud of it. I know that they were very much concerned when I left. They were happy for me to be going to school because they had made it possible. But they were still concerned because it broke up the group. I'd been with them and we had all our things worked out and all. And it wasn't quite the same. You can't, back it was always, we were the three there that primarily crystallized that band. The banjo, the guitar and my play. We three were the ones who really always have, even today, climbed very closely together.
